nameStory: This tiny crab gets its name from living inside bivalve mollusks like clams and mussels - hence 'pea crab' for its small, pea-like size. The scientific name 'cylindrica' refers to its somewhat cylindrical or tube-shaped body, which helps it squeeze into the tight quarters of its mollusk hosts.
description: The cylindrical pea crab is a tiny parasitic crab that spends its entire adult life inside clams, mussels, and other bivalve mollusks along the New England coast. These pale, soft-bodied crabs are typically only about 1/4 to 1/2 inch across - roughly the size of a garden pea. Unlike typical hard-shelled crabs, their shell is thin and somewhat flexible, allowing them to live comfortably within their host's shell. You'll most likely encounter one when shucking oysters or steaming clams, where they appear as small, whitish or pinkish creatures.

idTips.label: Soft, thin shell
idTips.description: The shell feels noticeably soft and flexible compared to other crabs, almost leathery to the touch - an adaptation for living inside tight mollusk shells

idTips.label: Pale coloration
idTips.description: Body is typically whitish, pale pink, or cream-colored, lacking the darker pigments of free-living crabs

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Usually 1/4 to 1/2 inch across the shell - small enough to fit on your thumbnail with room to spare

idTips.label: Rounded body shape
idTips.description: Shell appears more cylindrical or tube-like than typical crab shapes, smooth to the touch without spines or bumps

idTips.label: Found inside bivalves
idTips.description: Always discovered inside clam, mussel, or oyster shells when you open them - never found crawling free on beaches

habitat: Found exclusively inside bivalve mollusks in New England's coastal waters, from shallow tidal zones to deeper offshore areas. You'll encounter them in clams and mussels harvested from mudflats, rocky intertidal areas, and subtidal zones throughout the region's marine environments.

seasonality.spring: Most easily found when harvesting spring shellfish like soft-shell clams and mussels. Crabs are active and may be more noticeable as their hosts filter-feed heavily during plankton blooms.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for discovering these crabs when steaming clams or shucking oysters during summer seafood feasts. The crabs are most active and easiest to spot during warm water months.
seasonality.fall: Still commonly found in harvested shellfish, though they may be preparing for winter dormancy. Fall oyster and clam harvests often reveal these tiny residents.
seasonality.winter: Less active and harder to spot as both the crabs and their hosts have slowed metabolism. Winter shellfish harvesting may still reveal dormant individuals tucked deep in their hosts.

funFact: Female pea crabs can actually change the taste of their host oyster or clam - many seafood connoisseurs consider finding one in your oyster to be good luck, claiming it makes the mollusk taste sweeter and more flavorful!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other pea crab species, but the cylindrical pea crab's more elongated, tube-like body shape sets it apart from the rounder common pea crab. Remember: cylindrical = more stretched out like a tiny sausage, not perfectly round like a pea.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called parasites, pea crabs don't usually harm their hosts significantly - they're more like freeloaders, sharing the food their host filters from the water. In some coastal communities, finding a pea crab in your seafood is considered a sign of freshness and quality.
compareHints: The cylindrical pea crab differs from the more common pea crab (Pinnotheres ostreum) by its more elongated, tube-like body shape rather than a perfectly round form. While other pea crabs are nearly spherical like their namesake vegetable, this species is noticeably stretched out lengthwise. Both share the same soft shell and pale coloration, but the cylindrical shape is diagnostic once you know what to look for.
